title: LLM.int8(): 8-bit Matrix Multiplication for Transformers at Scale
authors: Tim Dettmers, Mike Lewis, Younes Belkada, Luke Zettlemoyer

pages.title: Run a 175B model in 8-bit with zero quality loss

blocks.html: The problem. A 175B-parameter model in 16-bit precision needs about 350GB just to hold its weights — spread across eight or more 80GB A100 GPUs. That hardware cost put inference on the largest models out of reach for almost everyone outside a handful of well-funded labs.

The obvious fix, and why it failed. Halving the bits to 8-bit would halve the memory. But the naive way to do this — uniformly mapping each 16-bit value to one of 256 integer levels — was known to destroy large models: it cost 15-30 points of perplexity (a fluency measure; lower is better) and produced garbled text. By 2022 the field's working assumption was that very large Transformers simply could not be 8-bit quantized.

The contribution. LLM.int8() figures out exactly why naive quantization breaks at scale — a specific, newly characterized phenomenon called emergent outlier features — and routes around it with a mixed-precision matrix multiply: the rare troublesome dimensions are kept in 16-bit, everything else runs in 8-bit. The payoff is striking:
We develop a procedure for Int8 matrix multiplication ... which enables inference in LLMs with up to 175B parameters without any performance degradation.

The result in one sentence. Zero loss in zero-shot accuracy for models up to 175B, at roughly half the memory — shipped as the open-source bitsandbytes library, now the load_in_8bit=True flag in HuggingFace Transformers.

The goal. Take a tensor of 16-bit floats and represent it with 8-bit integers (256 possible values), storing one extra scaling number so you can recover an approximation. This halves memory and lets the matmul run on NVIDIA Tensor Cores' fast int8 path.
The standard recipe — absmax quantization:

Reading it term by term: $x_{\text{fp16}}$ is one entry of the tensor; $\max_i |x_i|$ is the largest absolute value in the tensor (or row/column), the scale; dividing by it maps everything into $[-1, 1]$; multiplying by 127 stretches that to the int8 range $[-127, 127]$; $\operatorname{round}$ snaps to the nearest integer. To dequantize, you reverse it: multiply the integer by $\max_i|x_i| / 127$.

A worked example. Suppose a row is $[0.1, -0.3, 0.2, 5.0]$. The absmax is 5.0, so the scale is $127/5.0 = 25.4$. The values quantize to $[3, -8, 5, 127]$. Dequantizing $3$ gives $3/25.4 \approx 0.118$ — fine. The problem appears when the small values are much smaller than the outlier: with absmax 5.0, a true value of 0.02 maps to $\operatorname{round}(0.02 \times 25.4) = 1$, and a true 0.01 maps to $0$ — distinct numbers collapse into the same bucket. Information is lost.

The core tension. int8 has only 256 levels. One huge value forces a coarse scale, and a coarse scale crushes the precision of everything small. As long as a tensor's values are all roughly the same magnitude this is fine; the trouble starts when a few values dwarf the rest. The next section shows that is exactly what happens in big Transformers.

The central empirical discovery. Starting around the 6.7B-parameter scale, Transformer hidden states develop a handful of emergent outlier features — specific dimensions of the activation vectors whose values are systematically enormous, sometimes ~20x larger in magnitude than every other dimension.

A picture to hold in your head. A hidden state is a vector of, say, 12,288 numbers. In a small model they are all comparable in size. In a large model, maybe 6 of those 12,288 dimensions are routinely 20x bigger than the rest — towering spikes in an otherwise flat landscape. These spikes appear in the same dimensions across different sentences.
Four properties the paper establishes:

items: Sparse: they occupy only about 0.1% of feature dimensions.
Systematic: the same dimensions produce outliers across different inputs and across many layers — they are a fixed structural feature of the trained model, not random noise.
Critical: zeroing them out (instead of quantizing them) collapses model quality. So you cannot simply clip or discard them — the model genuinely uses them.
Emergent with scale: small models do not have them; they appear abruptly as the model grows past ~6.7B params and as validation perplexity drops below a threshold.

blocks.html: Why this explains the failure. A single int8 scale must cover both the giant outliers and the tiny normal values. The outliers dominate the scale; the normal values — which carry most of the actual information — get quantized into a few coarse buckets and effectively erased. That is the 15-30 point perplexity collapse. The fix has to treat the two populations differently.

The plan. Do not force one number format on the whole matrix multiply. Split each matmul into two paths: a tiny, accurate 16-bit path for the outlier dimensions, and a big, cheap 8-bit path for everything else. Then add the two partial results.

items: Scan the input activations and flag the outlier feature dimensions — the few columns whose values exceed a magnitude threshold (the paper uses 6.0).
Pull those outlier columns (and the matching weight rows) out and compute their contribution in full 16-bit — accurate, and cheap because the slice is only ~0.1% of the matrix.
Sum the two partial outputs to get the final 16-bit result.

blocks.html: The second key trick — vector-wise quantization. Even for the non-outlier path, one global scale is too coarse. LLM.int8() gives the weight matrix a separate scale per row and the activation matrix a separate scale per column, then corrects for both after the integer matmul:

Reading it term by term: $A_{\text{int8}}$ and $B_{\text{int8}}$ are the int8 activation and weight matrices; their integer product is $C_{\text{int8}}$. $c_x$ is the vector of per-column activation scales, $c_w$ the vector of per-row weight scales; their outer product $c_x \otimes c_w$ gives a per-element rescaling factor that converts each integer entry back to a 16-bit value. Because each row and column has its own scale, a large value in one row no longer crushes the resolution of a neighboring row.

Why split rather than just use vector-wise scaling? Vector-wise scaling alone handles ordinary spread, but the emergent outliers are so extreme (20x) that they would still dominate their own column's scale and wipe out the other values in that column. Only by physically removing the outlier dimensions into a 16-bit side-path can the int8 path stay clean. The two ideas are complementary.
Implementation. The whole thing is a custom CUDA kernel. The 16-bit detour is cheap because outliers are sparse; the int8 path delivers the memory savings.

The test. Measured on OPT models from 125M up to 175B across a battery of zero-shot tasks — LAMBADA (last-word prediction), PIQA (physical commonsense), HellaSwag (sentence completion), WinoGrande (pronoun resolution).

The result. LLM.int8() matches 16-bit accuracy at every scale tested, including 175B. Naive int8 (and even vector-wise int8 without the outlier split) degrades sharply right at the ~6.7B threshold where the outliers emerge — a clean confirmation that the outliers are the cause and the mixed-precision split is the cure.

The honest trade-off. Memory drops ~50% at inference. Speed is comparable to 16-bit, not faster — the mixed-precision path's overhead roughly cancels int8's per-matmul speedup. The win is memory and accessibility, not raw throughput: you can now fit a model you previously could not afford the GPUs for.

The immediate effect. Before LLM.int8(), running a 30B+ model locally meant serious multi-GPU hardware. After it, a single 24GB consumer GPU could load OPT-30B, and two could hold OPT-66B. The open-source community could finally run the large models it was sharing, not just admire them.

The lineage. LLM.int8() opened the low-bit era. Its descendants include GPTQ and AWQ (post-training 4-bit weight quantization), and most directly QLoRA, which builds on bitsandbytes' 4-bit kernels to keep a frozen base in 4-bit while fine-tuning 16-bit LoRA adapters on top. The straight line from LLM.int8() through QLoRA is the technical foundation for the entire 2023-2024 era of fine-tuning large models on commodity hardware.

The conceptual legacy. The deeper contribution is the discovery that scale produces qualitatively new structure — emergent outlier features that simply do not exist in smaller models. That observation reframed quantization research: you cannot reason about a 175B model by extrapolating from a 125M one, because new phenomena switch on along the way.
